alternatives.cost: None to adopt, everything to reimplement around it.
alternatives.covers: In-process memoization keyed on hashable arguments, zero dependencies.
alternatives.gap: In-process only: no persistence across runs, so the entire point (re-running review on an unchanged PR without re-paying the orchestration) is lost. No conditioning, no tiers, no telemetry.
alternatives.name: functools.lru_cache / functools.cache (stdlib)

alternatives.cost: New dependency; the domain logic stays hand-written regardless.
alternatives.covers: Persistent on-disk cache with TTL, eviction, and tagging; the closest real competitor for the storage half.
alternatives.gap: Stores bytes under keys; the tiered lookup chain (exact -> normalized -> semantic with per-tier replay accounting and the forced-live guard) and the conditioning fingerprint are still ours. Adopting it would trade ~40 lines of JSON persistence for a new third-party dependency with its own SQLite locking semantics, for no behavioral gain.
alternatives.name: diskcache

alternatives.cost: New dependency for the smallest solved piece.
alternatives.covers: In-memory TTL and LRU eviction policies with a clean API.
alternatives.gap: Same as lru_cache: in-process only, no persistence, no tiers, no conditioning. Solves eviction, which is ~10 lines of ours.
alternatives.name: cachetools (TTLCache / LRUCache)

alternatives.cost: New dependency; semantics mismatch means fighting the API.
alternatives.covers: Disk-backed memoization of function calls, aimed at expensive recomputation.
alternatives.gap: Keys on function arguments by pickling; the conditioning tuple and tiered keys do not map onto argument pickling, and the anti-loop replay accounting has no hook. Built for numpy-scale recomputation, not verdict replay with safety guards.
alternatives.name: joblib.Memory

evidence: Read review_cache.py in full (507 ln). grep -rn 'lru_cache|diskcache|cachetools|joblib' tools/review/ returns only the E-0001 trigger pattern naming functools.lru_cache as a perf-tuning signal, not a used dependency. tests/test_review_cache_tiers.py (33 tests) pins the tier/conditioning/anti-loop/trigger behavior no library provides.
migration_loc: Keep as-is (0 lines). The storage half (~40 lines of JSON load/save) is the only piece a library could replace; not worth a dependency.
recheck: grep -rn 'import diskcache|import cachetools|from cachetools|joblib' tools/review/ requirements*.txt -- if a cache dependency appears, re-evaluate whether the storage half should move onto it.
strongest_counterargument: diskcache is genuinely good at the storage half and its SQLite backend handles concurrent writers, which our JSON file does not: two panel runs racing on the same decision-cache.json can clobber each other's stores (last write wins). Today that failure mode costs at most a lost cache entry (fail-open to a live run), never a wrong verdict, which is why it was accepted; if concurrent panel runs become common, revisit.
what_ours_does: ~507 ln: tiered decision cache (exact/normalized/semantic keys, full conditioning fingerprint, anti-loop forced-live guard, per-tier telemetry, JSON persistence with eviction) + trigger-conditioned aspect execution (explicit named triggers over file-type/diff-size/risk signals) + Table 11-3 expected-calls-per-review accounting, all stdlib-only.
why: Keep-ours. No existing cache library implements the domain semantics this module exists for: three lookup tiers (exact / normalized / semantic) each gated on a full conditioning tuple (registry fingerprint + file-type context + external-backend mode + prior findings), an anti-loop guard that forces a live run after MAX_REPLAYS consecutive non-exact replays, per-tier telemetry, and Table 11-3 expected-calls accounting with trigger-conditioned aspect execution. Those are the load-bearing behaviors; any library adoption would keep all of them hand-written around a dumber store, which is the worst of both.
